pack.title: Heat flow through layered building walls

provenance.notes: Layer dimensions and conductivities are chosen for this pack so that every numerical question depends on the supplied figure rather than on remembered material data.

repairs.reason: Three questions carried narrowing leaks. q1 and q3 restated one invariance fact between them, q1 disclosed that the guidance is set on a U-value (which is how q5 must be answered), and q6 disclosed how Figure 2 splits its resistance between its layers (which is most of what q5 computes).

blocks.text: Heat flow through layered building walls

When the two sides of a wall are held at different temperatures, heat flows steadily from the warmer side to the cooler one. In the steady state the rate of flow no longer changes with time, and the same quantity of heat passes through every layer of the wall each second. The flow is driven by the temperature difference across the wall and is opposed by the wall's thermal resistance.

blocks.caption: Figure 1. A single-layer wall. Heat passes from the warm side to the cool side at a steady rate.

blocks.latex: R = d / lambda;   Q = A * dT / R_total
blocks.caption: Thermal resistance of one layer, and the resulting rate of heat flow through the wall.

legend.meaning: thermal resistance of a layer per unit area, in square metre kelvin per watt
thickness of the layer in metres
conductivity of the layer's material in watts per metre kelvin
temperature difference between the two sides in kelvin
rate of heat flow in watts

blocks.text: A wall built from several layers behaves like a chain: the same heat passes through each layer in turn, and the resistances of the layers are added together to give the total resistance of the wall. Because the resistances are added, the order in which the layers are arranged does not change the total. A layer of low conductivity contributes a large resistance even when it is thin, while a thick layer of high conductivity may contribute very little.

blocks.caption: Figure 2. A two-layer wall of area 18 square metres, with the warm side held 20 kelvin above the cool side.

parts.label: Brick layer
parts.detail: thickness 0.24 m, conductivity 0.60 watts per metre kelvin

parts.label: Insulation layer
parts.detail: thickness 0.08 m, conductivity 0.05 watts per metre kelvin

blocks.text: Because the total resistance is a sum of positive terms, it is always larger than the resistance of any single layer taken alone. Adding a further layer can therefore only reduce the rate of heat flow, never increase it. Doubling the thickness of one layer doubles that layer's resistance, but it does not double the total resistance of the wall, because the other layers are unchanged.

Performance is usually quoted not as a resistance but as a U-value: the rate at which heat crosses one square metre of the wall for each kelvin of temperature difference, which is one divided by the total thermal resistance. Because it is stated per square metre and per kelvin, a wall’s U-value does not depend on how large the wall is or on how cold the day is. The guidance this text follows treats an external wall as adequate when its U-value does not exceed 0.28 watts per square metre kelvin.

questions.stem: A store room has a single-layer wall of area 24 square metres, 0.14 metres thick, made of a material whose conductivity is 0.35 watts per metre kelvin. On the day in question there are 12 kelvin across it. According to the text, what is the wall’s U-value?

supportSpans.quote: the rate at which heat crosses one square metre of the wall for each kelvin of temperature difference, which is one divided by the total thermal resistance

questions.explanation: The single layer resists its thickness divided by its conductivity: 0.14 ÷ 0.35 = 0.4 square metre kelvin per watt. The U-value is one divided by that total resistance, so it is 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5 watts per square metre kelvin. The wall’s area and the day’s temperature difference are given but do not enter: the text states the U-value per square metre and per kelvin precisely so that it depends on neither.

a.reason: 0.4 is the wall’s thermal resistance, not its U-value. The text defines the U-value as one divided by the total resistance, so the two are reciprocals and cannot be the same number.

c.reason: Multiplying by the day’s 12 kelvin gives the heat crossing a square metre on that particular day. The U-value is stated for each kelvin of difference, so the temperature difference has already been divided out.

d.reason: 720 watts is the rate of heat flow through the whole wall, A × dT ÷ R. That is a quantity in watts for this wall on this day; the U-value is in watts per square metre kelvin and is the same whatever the wall’s size or the weather.

hints.text: Work out the layer’s thermal resistance first, from its thickness and its conductivity.
Find the sentence that says what a U-value is in terms of the total resistance, and read it as an instruction.
Two of the four numbers you are given play no part at all — decide which before you calculate.

questions.stem: What is the rate of heat flow through the wall shown in Figure 2?

supportSpans.quote: R = d / lambda;   Q = A * dT / R_total
thickness 0.24 m, conductivity 0.60 watts per metre kelvin
the resistances of the layers are added together to give the total resistance of the wall

questions.explanation: Each layer resists in proportion to its thickness and in inverse proportion to its conductivity: the brick gives 0.24 ÷ 0.60 = 0.4 and the insulation 0.08 ÷ 0.05 = 1.6, a total of 2.0. The wall is 18 square metres with 20 kelvin across it, so the flow is 18 × 20 ÷ 2.0 = 180 watts.

b.reason: 225 watts uses the insulation layer’s resistance alone. The brick resists as well, and the text says the layers’ resistances are added.

c.reason: 900 watts uses the brick layer’s resistance alone, which leaves out the layer carrying most of the resistance.

d.reason: 1125 watts divides by the two thicknesses added together. It is the resistances that are added, and a resistance is a thickness divided by a conductivity.

hints.text: Work out each layer’s resistance before you go near the heat flow.
The text says how the two resistances combine into one figure for the wall.
Then multiply the area by the temperature difference and divide by that figure.

questions.stem: A builder proposes moving the insulation layer of the wall in Figure 2 from the cool side to the warm side, keeping both layers otherwise identical. According to the text, what effect does this have on the wall’s U-value?

options.text: It falls, because insulation is more effective on the warm side.
It rises, because the brick can then hold more heat.
It is unchanged, because resistances are added and a sum ignores the order of its terms.
It cannot be judged without knowing which side is the warmer on the day in question.

supportSpans.quote: Because the resistances are added, the order in which the layers are arranged does not change the total.

questions.explanation: The wall behaves like a chain: the same heat passes through each layer in turn and the layers’ resistances are added. Addition does not depend on the order of what is added, so the total resistance is exactly what it was, and the U-value with it.

a.reason: The text gives insulation no special relationship to either face. A layer’s resistance is its thickness divided by its conductivity wherever it sits in the wall.

b.reason: Storage plays no part in the steady state, where the rate of flow no longer changes with time and the same heat passes through every layer.

d.reason: A U-value is stated per kelvin of temperature difference, so it does not move with the weather. That is why the guidance can set one limit for all conditions.

hints.text: Find the sentence that says what the wall’s total resistance is made of.
The operation that combines the layers has a property worth naming.
Ask whether the order of the terms in a sum can change the sum.

questions.stem: A different wall has an area of 15 square metres with 16 kelvin across it. It is built from an outer layer 0.32 m thick of conductivity 0.80 watts per metre kelvin, and an inner layer 0.12 m thick of conductivity 0.15 watts per metre kelvin. What is the rate of heat flow through it?

supportSpans.quote: R = d / lambda;   Q = A * dT / R_total
the resistances of the layers are added together to give the total resistance of the wall

questions.explanation: Each layer resists its thickness divided by its conductivity: the outer layer 0.32 ÷ 0.80 = 0.4, the inner 0.12 ÷ 0.15 = 0.8, a total of 1.2. The wall is 15 square metres with 16 kelvin across it, so the flow is 15 × 16 ÷ 1.2 = 200 watts.

b.reason: 288 watts multiplies by the total resistance instead of dividing by it. Resistance opposes the flow, so it belongs under the line.

c.reason: 300 watts uses the inner layer’s resistance alone. The outer layer resists as well, and the text says the layers’ resistances are added.

d.reason: 600 watts uses the outer layer’s resistance alone, which leaves out the layer carrying most of the resistance.

hints.text: Work out each layer’s resistance before you go near the heat flow.
The text says how two resistances combine into one figure for the wall.
Then multiply the area by the temperature difference and divide by that figure.

questions.stem: Does the wall shown in Figure 2 meet the guidance the text sets?

options.text: Yes, though with very little to spare.
No; its U-value is nearly twice the greatest the guidance allows.
No; its U-value is more than ten times the greatest the guidance allows.

supportSpans.quote: treats an external wall as adequate when its U-value does not exceed 0.28 watts per square metre kelvin
thickness 0.08 m, conductivity 0.05 watts per metre kelvin

questions.explanation: The two layers resist 0.4 and 1.6, so the wall’s total resistance is 2.0 and its U-value is one divided by that, or 0.5 watts per square metre kelvin. The guidance allows no more than 0.28, and 0.5 is close to twice that. The wall does not meet it.

a.reason: A comfortable pass would need a total resistance well above 3.5. This wall reaches 2.0, and a larger U-value is a worse wall, not a better one.

b.reason: The wall is not marginal in either direction. Its U-value misses the limit by roughly the limit again, which is not a near miss.

d.reason: Ten times the limit would be a U-value of nearly 3, which is a total resistance of about a third. The insulation layer alone resists more than that.

hints.text: The guidance is written against a quantity the text defines from the total resistance; find it first.
Work out the wall’s total resistance, then turn it into that quantity.
Compare what you get with the greatest value the guidance allows, and by how much.

questions.stem: A different wall is built from an outer layer 0.30 metres thick of conductivity 1.20 watts per metre kelvin and an inner layer 0.03 metres thick of conductivity 0.04 watts per metre kelvin. The inner layer is replaced by one of the same material but twice as thick. According to the text, what happens to the wall’s total thermal resistance?

options.text: It doubles, because the resistance of the layer that changed doubles.
It is unchanged, because the material is the same as before.

supportSpans.quote: the resistances of the layers are added together to give the total resistance of the wall
Doubling the thickness of one layer doubles that layer's resistance, but it does not double the total resistance of the wall, because the other layers are unchanged.

questions.explanation: The outer layer resists 0.30 ÷ 1.20 = 0.25 and the inner 0.03 ÷ 0.04 = 0.75, a total of 1.00 square metre kelvin per watt. Doubling the inner layer’s thickness doubles its resistance to 1.50, so the total becomes 1.75. The rise is 0.75 on a total of 1.00 — three quarters.

a.reason: The layer that changed does double, but the outer layer is untouched and still contributes what it did before. The text says this explicitly: doubling one layer does not double the wall.

c.reason: A quarter is what the wall would gain if the outer layer were the one doubled. It is the thin inner layer that carries three quarters of the resistance, because its conductivity is thirty times lower.

d.reason: Resistance is thickness divided by conductivity, so thickness is half of what fixes it. Keeping the material and changing the thickness changes the layer’s resistance.

hints.text: Work out each layer’s resistance before and after the change, then compare the two totals.
The thin layer is not the small contributor here — divide its thickness by its conductivity and see.
Express the increase as a fraction of the original total, not of the layer that changed.
